title: Filtered search, the trap everyone hits
summary: At identical 5.1 percent selectivity, post-filter recall ranged from 0.199 to 0.974 depending only on how the filter related to the query. The standard k over s arithmetic describes just the uncorrelated case, and the dangerous failure returns too few results rather than bad ones.
html:
Fourteen days of index machinery, all of it answering the question "what are the nearest vectors to this query". No production system asks that question. They ask:

nearest vectors to this query
  WHERE tenant_id = 'acme'
    AND created_at > '2026-01-01'
    AND doc_type IN ('policy', 'runbook')

Your ANN index knows nothing about any of that, and the obvious ways to bolt it on both fail in ways worth understanding precisely.

The two obvious strategies

Post-filter: run the ANN, discard results that fail the predicate. Simple, no index changes, works with any library.

Pre-filter: evaluate the predicate first, then brute-force the survivors. Always correct, and it is Day 15's linear scan with extra steps.

The standard advice is that post-filtering breaks when the filter is selective, and the standard arithmetic is this: if a fraction s of the corpus passes, then retrieving K candidates yields about K * s survivors, so you need K of roughly k / s to end up with k results.

At one percent selectivity and k=10 that says retrieve a thousand. Clean, memorable, and it describes only one of the three situations you will actually meet.

I measured it and was wrong about the direction

I expected correlated filters to make post-filtering worse. Tenants write about their own things, so a tenant's documents cluster in embedding space, and I assumed that clustering would starve the filter. The opposite happened.

The corpus is 6,200 documents with real category labels, and those categories are genuinely clustered: within-category pairs are 4.3 times more similar than the corpus average. Three filters, all at the same 5.1 percent selectivity, differing only in how the filter relates to the query. At K=100 retrieved:

filter                                survivors   recall@10
query-aligned (search my own category)     46.3       0.974
random subset of the same size              4.9       0.490
query-opposed (a category I am not in)      2.4       0.199

Identical selectivity. Recall spanning 0.199 to 0.974.

Note the middle row first: 4.9 survivors against the 5.1 the uniform formula predicts. The standard arithmetic is correct, and it is correct only for a filter uncorrelated with the query, which is the one case that never happens.

The aligned row got nine times more survivors than the formula says, and the reason is obvious in hindsight. When the filter selects the region the query is already pointing at, the globally nearest documents are mostly inside the filter anyway. The filter is keeping what the ANN was going to return. Correlation helps.

Where the trap actually is

So the dangerous case is not a correlated filter, it is a filter correlated with the corpus but pointing away from the query. Searching for a networking question inside the cooking tenant. The ANN dutifully returns the best networking documents, every one of them from the wrong tenant, and the filter deletes all of them.

Watch how much work that case needs:

K retrieved    aligned    random    opposed
        100      0.974     0.490      0.199
        500      1.000     0.998      0.625
       1000      1.000     1.000      0.885
       2000      1.000     1.000      0.990

To reach 0.99 the aligned case needs about 500 candidates and the opposed case needs 2,000. Four times the work, at identical selectivity, decided entirely by something your query planner cannot see.

And it is worse than the averages suggest. At K=100 with the opposed filter, 91 percent of queries returned fewer than ten results at all. Not badly ranked, short. The system returns three documents and nothing indicates anything went wrong.

What to take from this

Selectivity alone does not predict post-filter behaviour, and sizing K from k / s will be wrong in both directions: wasteful when your filters align with your queries, dangerously optimistic when they do not.

The quantity that matters is the relationship between the filter and the query, which is a property of your workload rather than your data. You cannot read it off a schema. You have to look at real traffic and ask whether people usually search for things their filter contains.

Mostly they do, which is why post-filtering survives in production despite the arithmetic predicting disaster. A support engineer searching their own tenant's runbooks is the aligned case. The opposed case is rarer, and it fails silently and completely, which is a bad combination.

The one filter you are not allowed to get wrong

Everything above treats a missing result as a quality problem. One class of predicate is different, and it is worth separating now rather than when Day 75 covers it properly.

A tenant id or a permission check is not a relevance filter, it is an access control boundary. Post-filtering is still correct there, since you discard what the user may not see before returning anything. But the failure modes change character completely: a filter applied in the wrong place, or applied to the generated answer rather than to retrieval, means a user receives content from another tenant. The retrieval quality question becomes a disclosure question.

The rule that follows is simple and worth adopting before you need it. Security predicates are evaluated inside retrieval and never afterwards by something downstream, and never by the model. Everything else in this lesson is a performance discussion. That one is not.

Pre-filtering, and the gap in the middle

Pre-filtering is immune to all of this and has its own wall. One percent of a billion vectors is ten million, which is Day 15's problem at a tenth of the scale: still a linear scan, still bandwidth bound, still too slow.

So the two strategies cover the extremes:

  • Very selective filters (hundreds of survivors): pre-filter and brute force. Exact, cheap, done.
  • Very unselective filters (most things pass): post-filter. Few results are discarded and the arithmetic barely matters.
  • Everything in between: pre-filtering is too slow and post-filtering is unreliable in a way that depends on a workload property you probably have not measured.

That middle band is where most real predicates live, and it is the entire reason filtered ANN is a research area rather than a configuration flag. Tomorrow is what the good engines do about it: filter-aware traversal, where the predicate is evaluated during the search rather than before or after it.
exercise:
1. Classify your own filters. Take the three or four predicates your system actually uses and label each one aligned, random or opposed with respect to typical queries. Tenant scoping is usually aligned. A date range is usually close to random. A filter users set to deliberately look outside their usual area is opposed. That labelling tells you more about your post-filter risk than any selectivity number.

2. Measure the survivor count, not the recall. On your own data, run your normal ANN retrieval with your real filter applied afterwards, and record how many results survive per query rather than how good they are. Then count what fraction of queries return fewer than k. That fraction is your silent-failure rate, and it is the number that will not appear in any dashboard you currently have.

3. Find your crossover. For your corpus size, compute how many vectors pass your most selective filter. If it is under about fifty thousand, pre-filtering and brute-forcing is simpler, exact and probably fast enough, and you can stop worrying about any of this. Work out the selectivity at which that stops being true.
